problem: DRL ObjectNav agents such as EmbCLIP trained in simulators can learn shortcuts (e.g. searching for the wall colour associated with the target room) and fail to generalise when such appearance cues change. Domain randomization needs simulator changes and is hard to apply post hoc.
motivation: Simulators contain hidden dataset biases, so agents may learn non-semantic shortcuts instead of real object-room priors. A feature-level fix that needs no simulator edits and can be described in free-form language would be flexible and cheap.
key_idea: Augment CLIP image embeddings at feature level by adding scaled differences between CLIP text embeddings of bias variations (e.g. 'red wall' minus 'blue wall'), so the policy cannot rely on the shortcut.
insight: Controlled o.o.d. tests show the failure is a true shortcut: deceptive changes (the learned colour moved to a wrong room) hurt most and give shorter episodes, because the agent goes straight to the learned colour and stops. Text-difference augmentation in CLIP space cuts the relative drop in success on 1-room changes from 69% to 23% at negligible cost (88 to 90 GPU-hours), showing the shared vision-language space allows semantic augmentation without images.
method: Shortcut o.o.d. test on ProcTHOR-10k: 3-room houses (kitchen, bedroom, living room), 9 target objects, identical object and surface appearances, windows and decorations removed, and a fixed room-to-wall-colour mapping in training (living=blue, kitchen=red, bedroom=green).
Test sets 0/1/2/3-room: increasingly many room wall colours permuted on unseen layouts, split into deceptive (learned colour moved to a non-target room) and nondeceptive changes.

L-B augmentation: I_LB = I_t + alpha*Delta(T), where Delta are all n(n-1) pairwise differences of CLIP text embeddings ('a photo of a {blue/red/green wall}'); one is randomly sampled each step (alpha=50).
Integration: one extra layer on the open-world EmbCLIP architecture (frozen CLIP ResNet-50 embedding fed directly to the RNN), followed by feature standardisation before the RNN.
Training: DD-PPO in AllenAct, 30M steps, reward shaped on distance-to-target progress with slack -0.01 and success +10, RGB only, 224x224.

setting.backbone: EmbCLIP (frozen CLIP ResNet-50 + RNN policy, trained with DD-PPO) with L-B augmentation layer
setting.training_data: 20 visually identical biased ProcTHOR-derived scenes, 9 target objects, 30M steps of RL; no extra data
setting.action_space: discrete: MOVEAHEAD 0.25 m, ROTATELEFT/RIGHT 30°, LOOKUP/LOOKDOWN 30°, DONE, with actuation noise
setting.privileged: none at test time; the bias variations (wall colours) are specified by the designer in text

numbers.eval_set_note: 1080 episodes per test set over 5 unseen layouts, wall colour permutations and 9 targets; 1-room test set (target room wall colour changed)
numbers.extra: trained on 20 biased scenes; alpha=50; the same paper's baseline EmbCLIP reached 45% SR and 0.22 SPL on 0-room and 14% and 0.04 on 1-room
numbers.evidence: Sec. Benefit of L-B: 'only a 23% relative drop in success (39% -> 30%) and 29% drop in SPL (0.17 -> 0.12)'

numbers.eval_set_note: 0-room reference test set (no wall colour change), L-B model

numbers_note: Results are mainly given in bar-chart figures; only some numbers appear in text. Percent values are printed as ints, SPL in 0-1 scale.
results: On the target-room wall-colour change, the L-B augmented agent's success drops only 23% (39%->30%) and SPL 29%, versus 69% (45%->14%) and 82% for plain EmbCLIP. Degradation is also smaller with more colour changes.
limitations: Only a simple wall-colour bias in a synthetic, heavily simplified ProcTHOR setup with few training scenes; conventional domain randomization could handle this case
alpha was tuned on this specific dataset and bias, and the bias variants must be known and described by hand
Absolute performance of the L-B agent is lower in-distribution (39% vs 45% SR), and no real-world or standard benchmark evaluation
